_note: DRAFT rounds aligned to Alberta PEW 8 Food Literacy (credible sources; advertising/social media; growth & development) and the microsite lesson. Thought Cafe drafts final content; MediaSmarts fact-checks.
curriculumHooks: Identify credible sources for nutritional information
Explore ways nutrition supports growth and development
Consider the role of social media and advertising in food choice

rounds.visual: A popular athlete holds a PeakFuel sports drink on a podium. No caption about the drink, just a wink and the logo.
rounds.feeling: Winning, status, and "athletes use this" cool, the drink borrows the athlete's credibility without saying what it does.
rounds.literalClaim: Nothing checkable. The athlete appears with the product; no statement is made about sugar, caffeine, electrolytes, or performance.
rounds.evidence: Marketing that targets youth can influence food choices without offering facts. An athlete selfie is not a credible nutrition source. Check the Nutrition Facts table (sugar, sodium, serving size) and guidance from a registered dietitian or a government / public health agency.
rounds.verify: Nutrition Facts table + registered dietitian, Health Canada, or Alberta Health Services, not the brand account.

rounds.headline: Clinically proven to boost focus by 40% before class
rounds.visual: Bright cereal box with a graph shooting upward and a lab-coat silhouette watermark.
rounds.feeling: Smart, school-ready, scientifically trusted, the packaging borrows the look of research.
rounds.literalClaim: The ad claims a 40% boost in focus that is clinically proven and guaranteed.
rounds.evidence: Health claims on packaging can influence food choices even when they overreach. A dramatic percentage with no named study is not reliable nutrition information. Compare similar cereals using Nutrition Facts tables, calories, sugar, sodium, and serving size all matter.
rounds.verify: Nutrition Facts table (watch serving size). Cross-check with Health Canada or a registered dietitian, not the box front.

rounds.visual: Teens laughing around a campfire. Coolers of Northlake bottles sit in frame. No voice-over about the water.
rounds.feeling: Belonging, friendship, and summer freedom, the brand wants to feel like your crowd.
rounds.literalClaim: No product claim. The ad sells belonging while the brand sits in the scene.
rounds.evidence: Advertising can shape food and drink choices by selling identity, not nutrition. Soft sell makes no claim you can check. During adolescence, a stage of rapid growth, brands often target that need to belong. For real nutrition questions, use credible sources, not lifestyle ads.
rounds.verify: Ask what is said about the product versus the lifestyle. Credible sources: registered dietitians; government or public health agencies.

rounds.headline: A source of calcium and vitamin D
rounds.body: Calcium and vitamin D help maintain bones and teeth.
rounds.visual: Yogurt cup with a regulated nutrient-function line about bones; Nutrition Facts panel visible on the side.
rounds.feeling: Responsible and growth-smart, framed as a sensible choice for developing bodies.
rounds.literalClaim: The product is a source of calcium and vitamin D, which help maintain bones and teeth.
rounds.evidence: Nutrient function claims like this can be allowed in Canada when criteria are met. That matters for growth and development: adolescents need additional calcium and vitamin D to support bone growth. Still read the Nutrition Facts table, amount per serving depends on serving size, and compare sugar across similar products.
rounds.verify: Nutrition Facts table (calcium, vitamin D, sugar, serving size). Confirm with Health Canada nutrient claims guidance or a registered dietitian / public health agency.

rounds.visual: A streamer's desk with a ZapEnergy can always in frame. Chat spam of the brand emoji. No spoken claim about the drink.
rounds.feeling: Gamer identity and "always on" energy, the can becomes part of the scene you already like.
rounds.literalClaim: No claim is made. The product is placed in entertainment so the brand stays familiar.
rounds.evidence: Social media and entertainment marketing influence food choices by repetition, not evidence. Familiarity is not proof the drink supports growth or well-being. Check caffeine, sugar, sodium, and serving size on the Nutrition Facts table.
rounds.verify: Did anyone state a fact, or did the can just appear? Label + government / public health guidance, not the stream.

rounds.headline: Clean ingredients. Fuel your body.
rounds.body: Made for the way you move. #CleanFuel
rounds.visual: Soft daylight product shot with leafy props. No numbers, no Nutrition Facts, no study cited.
rounds.feeling: Clean, virtuous, high-performance wellness, "clean" and "fuel" sound like nutrition advice.
rounds.literalClaim: No specific, checkable nutrition claim (no amounts, no named nutrients, no verified health outcome). "Clean" and "fuel your body" are brand voice.
rounds.evidence: Nutritional information is more reliable from registered dietitians and government or public health agencies than from a brand's social feed. "Clean" marketing has a commercial motive and is not a substitute for the Nutrition Facts table.
rounds.verify: Sort as brand marketing. Check ingredients and Nutrition Facts; compare with a registered dietitian or public health source.

rounds.headline: Diet culture called. We hung up.
rounds.body: A wink at "guilt-free" soda ads, then the joke lands: it's still a flavoured drink.
rounds.visual: Over-the-top parody of wellness soda ads, poking fun at hard-sell diet promises.
rounds.feeling: In-on-the-joke confidence, flattering teens who see through diet-culture ads.
rounds.literalClaim: The joke mocks other ads. It does not offer a checkable claim about nutrition benefits.
rounds.evidence: Parody still sells a brand feeling. For sugar, calories, and serving size, and for what actually supports growth, use the Nutrition Facts table and credible public health sources, not the punchline.
rounds.verify: Was anything factual asserted? Label + Health Canada / Alberta Health Services / registered dietitian.

rounds.headline: Flushes toxins in 3 days, I feel brand new
rounds.body: Link in bio. Not medical advice (but it works!!)
rounds.visual: Selfie with tea mug and sparkle filters; caption pushes a 3-day toxin flush.
rounds.feeling: Quick fix, transformation, and personal proof, the influencer's story stands in for evidence.
rounds.literalClaim: The ad claims the tea flushes toxins in three days and implies personal transformation.
rounds.evidence: Food choices can be influenced by social media diet trends that include misinformation. "Detox" / "flush toxins" claims are not supported by credible evidence. Testimonials are not a substitute for registered dietitians or government / public health agencies.
rounds.verify: Health Canada or Dietitians of Canada on detox products. Prefer sources without a product to sell.
